summary.text: An ocean front is a boundary between two distinct bodies of water that differ in properties such as temperature, salinity or density.
Fronts can be as narrow as a few hundred metres or as wide as tens of kilometres, and while most form and fade quickly, some last a long time.
Satellites that measure sea-surface height now locate fronts by their strong currents, showing that Southern Ocean fronts are no longer circumpolar and vary with place and time.

facts.label: Width
facts.value: A few hundred metres to tens of kilometres

facts.label: Visible sign
facts.value: A line of foam on the surface

items.prompt: A river empties into the sea. Along the line where the two waters meet, what difference creates the front?

options.label: Fresh river water meeting salty seawater
Fast wind over the river, calm over sea
Deep river water meeting shallow seawater
Clear river water meeting murky seawater

items.explain: In estuaries the fresh river inflow meets much saltier seawater, building strong salinity gradients that form a salinity front.

items.prompt: From a boat near a river mouth, you spot a sharp line of foam stretching across the water. What is it most likely marking?

options.label: A sandbar lying just below the surface
A school of fish feeding near the top
Two water masses converging at a front
A spill of soap washed off the shore

items.explain: Surface fronts can often be seen as a line of foam formed where the two water masses converge.

items.prompt: Fronts in estuaries tend to last only a short time compared with large ocean fronts. Why?

options.label: River water evaporates before it reaches the sea
They need a constant supply of energy to survive
Fish and boats churn them apart within hours
Sunlight heats both sides until they match

items.explain: Being small, they are not held in inertial balance, so they need a constant source of energy, which explains their short lifetime.

items.prompt: Early oceanographers mapped fronts from slow research cruises, combining data gathered over long periods. What sort of picture did that give?

options.label: A day-by-day record of each front's shifts
Exact positions updated every few hours
A detailed view of small estuary fronts only
An averaged view showing only broad structure

items.explain: Combining low-resolution cruise data took a long time, so the front positions were time-averaged and showed only the broad-scale structure.

items.prompt: An estuary has a very large tidal range, so its water is churned hard twice a day. What usually happens to fronts there?

options.label: The mixing generally stops fronts from forming
The strongest fronts on Earth form there
Fronts form but freeze in place for years
Tides have no effect on front formation

items.explain: Very large tidal ranges generally mix the waters and so inhibit front formation, although some smaller estuaries can form a front during flood tide.

items.prompt: Modern satellites can map ocean fronts around the whole globe. What do they measure to find them?

options.label: Cloud cover hanging over the sea
Radio calls from fishing boats
The number of whales at the surface
The height of the sea surface

items.explain: Continuous sea-surface height measurements reveal the strong currents or jets tied to fronts at high resolution in space and time.

paragraphs.heading: Where two waters meet
paragraphs.text: An ocean front is the boundary between two distinct water masses. A water mass is a body of water with its own physical properties, such as temperature and saltiness, or salinity. On either side of a front, the water differs in temperature, salinity or density, and in other ocean markers too. Fronts can be as narrow as a few hundred metres or as wide as tens of kilometres. Most appear and fade fairly quickly, but some last a long time.

paragraphs.heading: The old picture
paragraphs.text: Fronts were first mapped from measurements taken on research cruises, which gave only a coarse view. Those data took a long time to piece together, so the front positions they gave were averages over time that showed only the broad pattern. In the Southern Ocean this produced a picture of five fronts. Each was thought to circle Antarctica without a break, reach great depths and follow the shape of the seafloor.

paragraphs.heading: The view from space
paragraphs.text: Satellites now measure sea-surface height around the whole globe, all the time. From those readings scientists can pinpoint the strong currents, or jets, that run along fronts, in fine detail in both place and time. This allows a newer definition of a front as a place with a strong current. It also lets researchers track short-term changes and compare them with climate patterns such as El Niño. Seen this way, the Southern Ocean fronts no longer form full rings, and how many there are depends on where and when you look.

paragraphs.heading: How fronts form
paragraphs.text: The making of a front is called frontogenesis. Ocean currents, wind and the Coriolis force all play a part. For example, winds blowing toward the equator along a continent's west coast, or toward the pole along its east coast, can set up differences in how water moves up and down. These lead to what is called Ekman flow and can build upwelling fronts. In a similar way, western boundary currents can strengthen and produce fronts of their own.

paragraphs.heading: Fronts in river mouths
paragraphs.text: Some of the strongest fronts of all form in estuaries, where a river flows into the sea. There the fresh river water meets much saltier seawater, creating a salinity front. These fronts are small, so the Coriolis force has little effect on them. They need a steady supply of energy to survive, so they do not last long, but they can also form quickly. At the surface they can often be seen as a line of foam where the waters converge, or as a change in colour from the mud the river carries.

paragraphs.heading: Two estuary examples
paragraphs.text: Where tides are weak, the lighter fresh water spreads out to sea as a surface layer, especially as the tide goes out, and a plume front forms at its edge. Fronts like this occur in Chesapeake Bay and in front of the Mississippi, Amazon and Connecticut rivers. In some smaller estuaries a different front forms as the tide comes in. The incoming salt water dives under the fresh water and pushes it back, leaving a front shaped like a V.
